title: Seoul Street Food Guide: 20 Must-Try Snacks & Where to Find Them
description: 20 Must-Try Snacks & Where to Find Them
content:
The Immortal Heart of Seoul Street Food: Gwangjang Market

In a city as fast-paced as Seoul, where skyscrapers rise overnight and trends vanish in a blink, Gwangjang Market remains a steadfast guardian of Korean culinary heritage. Established in 1905, it stands as the city’s oldest and largest traditional market, an sprawling labyrinth where the air is perpetually thick with the scent of toasted sesame oil and sizzling batter. For the discerning traveler, Gwangjang is not just a place to eat; it is a sensory immersion into the very soul of the peninsula.

Despite a localized scandal in late 2025 regarding overcharging at select stalls, the market has entered 2026 with renewed transparency and undiminished energy. Locals and tourists alike continue to flock here for the unparalleled convenience of having the country’s most iconic dishes gathered under one historic roof. It serves as a vital cultural bridge, where you can rub shoulders with office workers during the frantic lunch rush or share a bench with elderly residents who have frequented the same vendors for decades.

Navigating Gwangjang requires a strategy of "small bites, many stops." The market is famously unpretentious, trading white tablecloths for heated benches and plastic stools. Here, the "famous and delicious" ethos of Korean dining is on full display. Whether you are seeking the comforting warmth of hand-cut noodles in the dead of winter or a quick, addictive snack between sightseeing stops at nearby Dongdaemun or Insadong, Gwangjang delivers a visceral food experience that modern malls simply cannot replicate.

The Crispy Legend: Bindae-tteok and the Art of Mung Beans

If Gwangjang Market had a signature scent, it would be the nutty, oily aroma of Bindae-tteok (savoury mung bean pancakes) hitting a hot griddle. Unlike the flour-based pancakes found elsewhere, these are crafted from mung beans ground on-site using traditional stone mills. The resulting batter is thick, textured, and fried to a deep golden brown, creating a contrast between a crunch that resonates and a center that remains soft and earthy.

These pancakes are traditionally served with a dipping sauce of soy, vinegar, and pickled onions, which provides a sharp, acidic counterpoint to the richness of the fried bean paste. At roughly ₩5,000 to ₩8,000 ($3.75 - $6.00) per pancake, it is one of the most cost-effective ways to fill up. For a complete experience, pair it with a bowl of makgeolli (Korean rice wine), as the fizzy, milky beverage is the traditional partner for all things fried in Korea.

💡 Pro Tip: Look for the stalls where you can see the stone mills actively grinding the beans. This ensures the batter is fresh and hasn't been sitting, which is key to achieving that signature "hashbrown-like" outer texture without it becoming soggy.

Master of the Blade: Kalguksu and the Netflix Phenomenon

Few dishes offer as much comfort as Kalguksu, or "knife-cut" noodles. These are not pulled or extruded; instead, the dough is rolled thin, folded, and sliced by hand with a massive cleaver, resulting in noodles with charmingly irregular shapes and a delightful "chew." The most sought-after bowl in the market is found at Gohyang Kalguksu, helmed by Cho Yonsoon. Her rise to global fame following the Netflix Street Food: Asia series has made her stall a pilgrimage site, but the quality remains remarkably consistent despite the crowds.

A steaming bowl of Mandu-kalguksu (noodles with dumplings) typically costs around ₩7,000 to ₩9,000 ($5.25 - $6.75). The broth is usually a clean, deep anchovy or vegetable stock, topped with roasted seaweed and scallions. While you wait—often up to 30 minutes during peak hours—you can watch Ms. Cho herself kneading and stretching the dough with a rhythmic precision that has been perfected over three decades of service.

For those visiting in the summer, the cold version, Bibim-guksu, is an essential alternative. These thin wheat noodles are tossed in a vibrant, spicy, and slightly sweet gochujang-based sauce, served with ice and julienned cucumbers. It provides a refreshing zing that cuts through the humid Seoul afternoons, proving that the market’s noodle masters are as adept with cold dishes as they are with hot broths.

Addictive Bites: Mayak Kimbab and Tteokbokki

The term "Mayak" translates to "narcotic" or "drug," but in the context of Mayak Kimbab, it refers to the addictive nature of these miniature rice rolls. Unlike their larger cousins, these are bite-sized seaweed rolls filled simply with carrots, pickled radish, and spinach, brushed generously with sesame oil. The secret lies in the mustard dipping sauce, which provides a sinus-clearing kick that keeps you reaching for "just one more." A bundle of these usually costs around ₩3,000 - ₩5,000 ($2.25 - $3.75).

Sitting nearby are the giant vats of Tteokbokki, the ubiquitous Korean street food of chewy rice cakes bathed in a thick, fiery red pepper sauce. At Gwangjang, the rice cakes are often thicker and chewier than the mass-produced versions found at subway exits. The sauce is a balance of heat and sweet, often accompanied by eomuk (fish cakes) that soak up the spicy gravy. Expect to pay about ₩4,000 - ₩6,000 ($3.00 - $4.50) for a generous portion.

If you are feeling adventurous, ask for Sundae (Korean blood sausage) alongside your tteokbokki. These sausages, filled with glass noodles and pig’s blood, are steamed and sliced, then dipped into the tteokbokki sauce or a side of salt and pepper. It is a savory, iron-rich staple that serves as a litmus test for true lovers of Korean street food. Together, these snacks form the "Holy Trinity" of market eating: spicy, salty, and incredibly satisfying.

The Modern Twist: Garlic Boy and Starbucks Gwangjang

While tradition reigns supreme, Gwangjang has recently embraced modern food trends. Garlic Boy is a standout example, serving a Korean take on garlic bread that is more akin to a savory cream puff. A pillowy bun is drenched in garlic butter and stuffed with a rich, velvety garlic cream. It is a messy, indulgent snack that represents the "New Seoul"—sweet, savory, and highly photogenic. These buns generally retail for approximately ₩5,000 ($3.75).

For a respite from the market's humidity and noise, the Starbucks Gwangjang offers a unique "secret" rooftop. Housed in a restored red-brick textile warehouse, this is not your average coffee shop. The design reflects the market's history, and the menu features exclusive items like the Honey Hotteok Latte. The rooftop terrace allows visitors to look down on the market’s corrugated roofs and pose behind the iconic Gwangjang Market Korean signage.

💡 Pro Tip: The Starbucks rooftop is one of the few places in the area with a clear view of the market's architectural transition. Visit at dusk when the market signs illuminate for the best photography lighting, and try the Byuldabang Lager if you're finished with caffeine for the day.

Handmade Traditions: Mandu and Hodo Kwaja

No visit is complete without a tray of Mandu (dumplings). These are hand-folded throughout the day, with fillings ranging from classic pork and chive (gogi mandu) to the punchy, fermented heat of kimchi mandu. You can have them steamed for a soft texture or pan-fried for a crispy bottom. A plate of six to eight dumplings usually costs ₩5,000 - ₩7,000 ($3.75 - $5.25). They are the perfect "bridge" food to share between larger meals.

Finally, for dessert, follow the scent of baking cake to a Hodo Kwaja stall. These walnut-shaped cakes are made from a sweet batter filled with either red bean paste or creamy custard, with a piece of actual walnut tucked inside. They are best eaten piping hot, straight from the mold. A small bag usually costs ₩3,000 - ₩5,000. It is the quintessential walking snack as you head toward the second floor to browse the traditional Hanbok (Korean dress) and textile shops.

Gwangjang Market is a bastion of culture that engages all five senses. Beyond the food, it is a place where you can find burial shrouds of fine white hemp, intricate silk for weddings, and the genuine smiles of vendors who have survived decades of change. It remains the ultimate one-stop shop for anyone wanting to taste the history of Seoul in a single afternoon.

Essential Information & Quick Facts

  • Location: 88 Changgyeonggung-ro, Jongno-gu, Seoul.
  • Subway: Jongno-5 Station (Line 1), Exit 8 or 9.
  • Hours: Daily 8:30 am – 6:00 pm (Food stalls often stay open later, until 11:00 pm).
  • Quiet Day: Mondays (many stalls take a break after the weekend).
  • Capacity: Approximately 65,000 visitors per day.
  • Budget: ₩15,000 - ₩25,000 ($12 - $20 USD) is enough for a massive multi-stall feast.
  • Nearby Attractions: Cheonggyecheon Stream, Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP), and Insadong.
